title: Audiences and Bruno's College Inn; the Birmingham job explained
summary: European fans act like Americans. At Bruno's College Inn students come on Sunday afternoons. The Birmingham job was a student's father's dance, where dance-band players admired the band.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: One Raymond. There will be another one. There will be another one. What would you say the main difference between European jazz fans and American jazz fans?

I really couldn't detect that much of a difference. In Europe, you have more people flocking around to see what's going on. Because, well, like they say, they're stars for jazz over there. And naturally, wherever you set up, you get a bigger following. But they react the same way as the people react right here, you know. I mean, they know it's a happy music and they're having a happy time listening to it, you know. Clapping and whistling and whatnot.
Let's see, who comes up there at Bruno's? Now, when I'm up there, I see people I know from around school. Tulane, Newcomb.

Yeah, well, I would say, well, the name of the place is Bruno's College Inn. So, naturally being right up in this section of town around Tulane and Newcomb, you have a lot of students from Newcomb and Tulane that go over there, you see. And during the school year, well, we'll play from 5 to 7. You see, it's pretty early in the evening. And from what I can understand, I think most of the students have to get back in dormitories at certain times. So we don't want to confine too much of that time to, you know, stay in over there. But we get a pretty good group in every Sunday afternoon. After school closes, well, we play later hours. We'll start at 7 and play till 9. And then you'll find you have more of an older group of people that come in to listen, you know. But during school time, we'll play from 5 to 7 on a Sunday, give them a chance to go listen to music. Then if they want to go catch a show downtown, they still got time, you see.
At parties, do you play for like young and old or like?

Young and old like, yeah. You have, I don't know, when you're playing that kind of music, the old just automatically turn young. So I guess you're playing for all young people really. Yeah, that's right.

I heard that Birmingham job, you couldn't remember anything about it, but from what I remember, that I was told, I think a girl who goes to school here, or had gone to school here, had a bunch over at Bruno's and she knows ice. And she had gotten her father to put up a pretty good bundle to bring the band up there for two hours and they followed a regular dance that they had at their house, didn't they?

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's right. Well, again too, now that goes back to the business angle, see, which I'm not too, too familiar with, but that's how we got to make the trip over there. Incidentally, we started playing, must have been, what time? 12, 12 o'clock, 3 o'clock, it was a ridiculous hour we started. But before this, they had a nice dance band there. I mean, these guys were strictly, you know, reading musicians that were very good. And one of the fellas, the guy who fronted his band was a trumpet man, and he played with Charlie Spivak's orchestra. And he had a bunch of young musicians and they played, you know, all nice dance music. But after they had knocked off, after their job was over, they went and asked the lady who was running the thing if it would be alright if they would stay and listen to the New Orleans band play. And she gave them permission to stay. So they all cluttered around the back of the bandstand and they actually went wild. I mean, you know, they said, well, how can you guys do this without having music in front of you? You know, they couldn't get over that. We're making this stuff up almost as we go along, you see. And they were pretty well pleased with the, you know, with the resolve. That is kind of hard to understand. Well, like I tell people, they want to know, what is jazz supposed to be? Or what is Dixie Landon? Dixie Landon. Now, the way I look at it, it's each musician is playing a solo simultaneously. You see, in other words, you're making your stuff up as you go along. In other words, these guys actually playing a solo together.
